answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
In theory, it is highly desirable to develop a global consequential accounting framework. And we believe that where emission impact data are publicly available, they should be reported when using the market-based approach. The ability to procure emissions reductions globally is also, in theory, very attractive. However, in practice it is extremely difficult to know whether a project was actually built, is additional and delivered the expected reductions if this is done very far away from the corporate making the procurement.

Previous attempts (e.g., CDM, Verra) to create such frameworks have failed and have often led to greenwashing. We see no reason to believe that a new global framework would be any different.

For this reason, using the market-based accounting approach to actively enable and finance new projects is preferable. At the same time, it would be beneficial if corporates using this method were required to consider and explain the additionality and emission impact of their procurements. This would encourage greater self-regulation and more responsible claims.

answers.label: Requiredness of the financial analysis test
Requiredness of the common practice test
Why selected tests should be included
answers.text:
First, it is unlikely that a single additionality test can be applied globally.

In the European market, the most robust additionality test is a regulatory one. If a project has already received government subsidies, corporates cannot be considered the primary enablers of that project.

A commonly held view is that only long-term contracts and/or bundled purchases of EACs and electricity should be considered additional. However, this would be a highly undesirable definition of additionality, as it would lock in existing market structures and effectively prevent the development of more flexible solutions tailored to SMEs, such as the one www.the0mission.dk is developing. In turn, this would slow down the deployment of new renewable energy projects.

The financial test is also problematic as it directly encourages building less efficient projects in worse locations.

The timing test is also extremely problematic. It is well known to delay projects, as developers are discouraged from taking early-stage risks if they must rely solely on confirmed demand before initiating project development. Also it prevents a secondary market for PPAs (no one would be able to claim additionality on a secondary PPA) which increases risks and discourages signing of PPAs altogether.

answers.label: Context on test feasibility
answers.text: A regulatory test is the only relevant test. It is easy observable - is already registered on the GoOs (in Europe) and avoids adding more bureaucracy and freezing markets.

answers.label: Additionality tests missing from the framework
answers.text: Only projects younger than 10-15 years should be able to passe the test as the project will likely be paid back after 10-15 years.

answers.label: Regions warranting different tests, with examples
answers.text: In Europe the regulatory test is highly desirable and easy implementable - in the Chinese market is it more questionable whether or not you can distinguish between projects mandated by the government and project not mandated by the government.
